extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, patent examiners, and judges (practitioners in patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Judicial statements of standards governing patentability, priority of invention, admissibility of evidence in patent office hearings, and statutory/technical requirements for specifications and claims — used when litigating or prosecuting patent applications and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4th rule — evidence filing requirement (text)
rubrics_metrics.description: "4th. That no evidence, statement or declaration, touching the matter at issue, shall be considered upon the said day of hearing, which shall not have been taken and filed in compliance with the rule: provided, that if either party shall be unable, from good and sufficient reason, to procure the testimony of a witness or witnesses within the above stipulated time, then it shall be the duty of said party to give notice of the same to the Commissioner of Patents, accompanied with statements of the cause of such inability; which last mentioned notice to the Commissioner shall be received by him ten days previous to the day of hearing aforesaid, viz: the day of next."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the explicit procedural rule governing what evidence may be "considered" at the hearing and the notice/proviso for inability to procure testimony; the proviso requires notice to be received ten days before the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of the 4th rule — reading v. considering evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition is not against the Commissioner's looking into or reading an informally transmitted deposition, but against his considering it on the day of hearing as evidence touching the matter at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner may read such informal material to ascertain contents, but must not treat it as evidence at the hearing day; this interpretation prevents a mechanical bar to judicial awareness while preserving the rule's procedural protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's power to postpone hearings to further justice
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing in the laws or the Commissioner's rules to prevent him from postponing the hearing of a cause if, in his opinion, the justice of the case should require it, especially to correct an irregularity in matters of form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner may postpone to allow cure of formal irregularities or to further justice; denying that power would improperly stifle justice. The rule's proviso does not itself compel or limit whether the Commissioner must receive testimony or postpone — he retains discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections must be timely made at hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to proceedings (such as insufficient notice to appear for deposition) that are not made at the hearing are considered waived and not available on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an appellant fails to raise an objection at the time of trial/hearing, appellate review will treat that ground as forfeited; raise procedural complaints promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of time for notice to appear
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of eleven days to appear for taking depositions (even when the travel distance was large, e.g., 400 miles) was held to be reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What counts as 'sufficient time' is factual and judged by reasonableness; short travel windows may nevertheless be reasonable depending on circumstances and should be challenged at hearing if claimed insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of appellate revision — confined to reasons of appeal and Commissioner's written grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (11th section act March 3, 1839) the revision on appeal is to be "confined to the grounds of his decision, fully set forth in writing, touching all the points involved by the reasons of appeal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An appeal is limited to the specific points raised in the reasons of appeal and the corresponding grounds the Commissioner put in writing; courts will not expand review to unrelated matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of a known mechanical equivalent is not an invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The substitution of a known mechanical equivalent (e.g., substituting a pinion for a band, or applying an endless screw to a quadrant) is not an invention within the meaning of the patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely exchanging one well-known mechanical device for another performing the same function is ordinarily not patentable; courts view such substitutions as ordinary skill rather than inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of a common mechanical power to a new machine does not necessarily constitute invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere application of a common mechanical power to a machine to which it had not before been applied is not necessarily an invention (e.g., applying an endless screw to steering machinery is analogous to applying it to a kitchen-jack).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the application makes the machine better, that alone does not confer patentability unless there is a true inventive contribution beyond ordinary application of known powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patents — invention may be only a new combination of known parts
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention may consist only of a new combination of some known mechanical principles or powers; where the particular combination produces a new and useful effect, that combination is the lawful subject of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual components being old does not preclude patentability if their particular combination yields a novel, useful result; the court must identify what the patentable 'combination' is and whether it was first invented by the claimant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie inference from making a machine — rebuttable presumption of inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that a person made the machine which contains the combination claimed is prima facie evidence that he was the first inventor of that combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inference can be rebutted by evidence showing the maker was working as an employee, for wages, and at the direction and for the benefit/expense of another (employer), or by other evidence of priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption about work-for-hire and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person fabricated a machine while working in his trade for wages for another's benefit, there is a presumption it was made according to the employer's directions; then the burden is on the fabricator to show the machine was not made according to those directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employment circumstances, who paid and who directed, are critical; claimants who were employees must rebut presumption to establish inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice and who reduced the invention to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to practice by a person who discovered the combination (or who directed and paid for its reduction) is material to inventorship; one who simply fabricates at another's request may not be the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess who conceived and who reduced to practice (and who directed/rewarded the reduction) to determine priority and inventorship; evidence of who conceived the principle and who implemented it is pivotal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay and acquiescence can defeat a claim of priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Long delay in claiming or applying for a patent and standing by while another applies for and obtains a patent are facts that rebut a claim of priority; extended acquiescence may indicate the claimant was not the first inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt assertion of rights and timely prosecution strengthen a priority claim; unexplained delay or passive conduct weakens it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and weight of evidence (competency, hearsay, interest, waiver)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain items (e.g., letters offered as evidence) may be inadmissible; depositions and statements must be competent; testimony of interested witnesses affects credit; parties can waive objections by agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Object to incompetent hearsay at the hearing; note that agreements between counsel can waive competency objections; witness interest affects credibility, not necessarily admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof to show priority — courts act on the evidence before the Patent Office
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner and the reviewing court act only upon the evidence before them; if the appellant had other evidence and did not produce it, the failure is his fault and weakens his claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must present their best admissible evidence at the administrative proceeding; appellate review is constrained to the administrative record and the evidence actually produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles versus embodiments — abstract principles are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle (an abstract idea) or an abstract is not patentable 'in the abstract'; an embodiment or application of the principle may be patentable, and at some point a principle applied becomes a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent protection requires a concrete, practical application/embodiment of a principle; mere discovery of a scientific principle without a practical application does not support a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use / printed publication destroys novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior public use destroys the right to a patent; prior description in a public work inconsistent with novelty can defeat patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of prior public use or a prior printed description/public work is damaging to novelty; novelty inquiries include both actual use and prior public disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result as a test of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The production of a new and useful result (the 'result' achieved) is a test of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether the claimed invention produces an effect or result beyond the predictable outcome of known elements; a new useful result supports patentability of a combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifications — statutory and substantive requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must conform to statutory requirements: must agree with the patent; drawings annexed are part of the specification; they have two objects; rules exist for preparing specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow statutory/formal rules when drafting specifications; include necessary drawings; ensure specification aligns with the claims/patent and satisfies the office's procedural rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifications — clarity, disclosure, and best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications must not be ambiguous; must distinguish what is old from what is new; should state the best mode of producing an effect; should describe everything essential and avoid useless descriptions or misuse of terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft specifications to clearly identify the novel aspects, disclose the best mode, include essential elements, avoid ambiguity and unnecessary matter; courts construe specifications liberally but will penalize vagueness or omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and adjudication of specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Specifications are to be liberally construed; they are construed by the court and judged as to scope and meaning by the court (and in part by juries when appropriate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect judicial construction of specification language in litigation; use clear, consistent terminology to reduce adverse constructions and disputes over scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a principle becomes a process or application
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between a principle and when that principle becomes a process (i.e., the threshold where an idea is implemented as a patentable process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate concrete steps, apparatus, or transformative application to show that a principle has been turned into a statutory "process" eligible for patent protection.
